title: Stimulation of acyl-CoA oxidase by alpha-linolenic acid-rich perilla oil lowers plasma triacylglycerol level in rats.
text_summary: 研究比较大鼠摄入牛脂、玉米油、富含α-亚麻酸的紫苏油和鱼油后，肝脏过氧化物酶体氧化及餐后甘油三酯的变化。鱼油和紫苏油均降低肝脏及血浆甘油三酯；鱼油显著增强过氧化物酶体β-氧化、过氧化氢酶和酰基辅酶A氧化酶（AOX）活性，紫苏油也在短期喂养中提高AOX活性及mRNA水平。AOX活性与餐后甘油三酯呈负相关，说明紫苏油可通过增加肝膜长链n-3多不饱和脂肪酸、促进AOX表达和活性，部分解释其降低餐后甘油三酯的作用。

Life Sciences 77 (2005) 1293–1306

                                                                                                            www.elsevier.com/locate/lifescie


Stimulation of acyl-CoA oxidase by a-linolenic acid-rich perilla oil
           lowers plasma triacylglycerol level in rats

                     Hye-Kyeong Kim, Haymie ChoiT

      Department of Food and Nutrition, Seoul National University, Shillim-dong, Kwanak-gu, Seoul 151-742, Korea

                                Received 5 August 2004; accepted 22 October 2004


Abstract

  The effect of dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) on hepatic peroxisomal oxidation was investigated
with respect to the postprandial triacylglycerol levels. Male Sprague–Dawley rats were fed semipurified diets
containing either 1% (w/w) corn oil, or 10% each of beef tallow, corn oil, perilla oil, and fish oil for 4 weeks and 4
days. Hepatic and plasma triacylglycerol levels were reduced in rats fed fish and perilla oil diets compared with
corn oil and beef tallow diets. The peroxisomal h-oxidation, catalase activity, and acyl-CoA oxidase (AOX)
activity were markedly increased by fish oil feeding. To a lesser extent, perilla oil elevated AOX activity in a 4-day
feeding although the effect gradually decreased in a 4-week feeding. Similarly, the mRNA levels were increased in
rats fed fish and perilla oils. AOX activity was negatively correlated with postprandial triacylglycerol levels. In
addition, the stimulation of AOX was highly associated with the content of long chain n-3 PUFA such as
eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) in hepatic microsome. These effects were evident
within 4 days of initiating feeding. Therefore, a-linolenic perilla oil exerts a similar effect to fish oil in stimulating
hepatic activity and gene expression of AOX by enriching long chain n-3 PUFA in hepatic membrane fraction,
which can partly account for the reduction of postprandial triglyceridemia.

Introduction

  Recent studies have shown that elevated triacylglycerol (TG) concentrations, especially in the
postprandial state, may be associated with the increased risk of coronary heart disease (Uiterwaal et al.,
1994; Zilversmit, 1995; Roche and Gibney, 1999). It has been established that fish oil suppresses plasma
triacylglycerol concentrations in both postprandial and fasting states in human (Roche and Gibney, 1999;
Kris-Etherton et al., 2002) and experimental animals (Ikeda et al., 2001; Murata et al., 2002). Enhanced
rate of fatty acid oxidation in the liver appears to be a crucial factor for the hypotriglyceridemic effect of
fish oil in fasting state (Yamazaki et al., 1987). The effect of fish oil has been ascribed to the constituent
long chain n-3  polyunsaturated  fatty  acid (PUFA) such  as  eicosapentaenoic  acid (EPA) and
docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) (Aarslands et al., 1990; Weber, 1999; Berge et al., 1999).
  Considering that a-linolenic acid (ALA) can be a precursor of these very long chain fatty acids, it
is plausible that dietary ALA exerts similar physiological effect as in the case of very long chain fatty
acids in fish oil. It has been reported that dietary fats rich in n-3 ALA such as linseed and perilla oils
increased hepatic fatty acid oxidation rate through both mitochondrial and peroxisomal pathways in
fasting state (Ide et al., 1996; Kabir and Ide, 1996). However, the studies have not been performed in
the postprandial state. The activity of peroxisomal oxidation systems is known to be enhanced by the
administration of various substances that induce a hypotriglyceridemic effect (Yamazaki et al., 1987;
Osumi and Hashimoto, 1979).
  The plasma  triacylglycerol and  lipoproteins  are synthesized mainly  in  the  liver. Microsomes
contain fatty acid desaturases and the enzymes catalyzing the synthesis of phosphatidic acid, key
compound of both triacylglycerol and phospholipid. Membrane fatty acids serve as modulator of the
biological processes such as eicosanoid production and  activation of membrane-bound enzymes
(Stubbs and Smith, 1984; Strum-Odin et al., 1987; Huang and Nassar, 1990). Therefore, the study
on the fatty acid composition of cell membrane is thought to be important for understanding the
effect of dietary fats on plasma triacylglycerol. However, information has been limited whether the
effect of n-3 fatty acids on peroxisomal h-oxidation and serum lipid is mediated through alteration
in the fatty acid composition of hepatic lipids. In this context, we compared the activity and mRNA
level of hepatic peroxisomal enzyme in perilla oil-fed rats with other dietary fats in postprandial
state. In addition, the relationships to the fatty acid composition of hepatic membrane lipid were
investigated.


Materials and methods

Animals and diets

   All animal procedures were approved by Laboratory Animal Center of Seoul National University.
Male Sprague–Dawley rats, supplied by Laboratory Animal Center of Seoul National University, were
individually caged with free access of water during the entire experimental periods. Two separate
experiments were conducted to compare the effects of dietary fat-feeding periods. In the first feeding
experiment, weanling rats were fed one of the five experimental diets for 4 weeks with 10 rats in each
group. In order to facilitate control of diet intake, all animals were adapted to a meal-eating regimen in
which one meal allowed access to food for a 3-h period (0900–1200 h). Experimental diets were

group. For 7 days prior to the experimental period of fat supplementation, all rats were adapted to the
3-h feeding regimen, receiving 1C diet to have similar fatty acid status by exhausting the stored fatty
acids. After this preliminary feeding, rats were fed one of five experimental diets described in long-
term feeding model only for 4 days. The fatty acid compositions of dietary fats are shown in Table 2.
To prevent autoxidation, a-tocopherol was supplemented in perilla oil (0.015%) and fish oil (0.019%),
based on peroxidizability index (Witting, 1974). In addition, meals were offered daily and diets were
stored in the freezer and replenished with N2 gas to minimize the peroxidation of lipids.

Sample preparation

  Rats were sacrificed by decapitation at 90–120 min after completion of the final meal. An aliquot
of each liver was quickly removed and snap frozen in liquid N2 and kept at  70 8C for mRNA assay.
About 5 g of each liver was homogenized in 5 volume of ice cold homogenizing buffer solution (154
mM KCl, 50 mM Tris–HCl, 1 mM EDTA buffer, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 600  g for 10 min to
prepare  post-nuclear  supernatant, which was used  for peroxisomal  assay. The  supernatant was
centrifuged at 10,000  g for 20 min, followed by recentrifugation of the supernatant at 105,000  g
for 60 min. The resulting pellet was considered the microsome and resuspended in cold storage buffer
(homogenizing buffer/glycerol, 80:20 v/v). The entire fractionation procedure was conducted at 4 8C.

Enzyme assays

  Hepatic peroxisomal h-oxidation capacity was measured as the cyanide insensitive fatty acyl-CoA-
dependent NAD reduction using palmitoyl-CoA as a substrate (Lazarow, 1981). Acyl-CoA oxidase (EC
1.3.3.6) activity was measured by the method of Osumi and Hashimoto (1978). The assay mixture (1 ml)
contained 0.82 mM 4-aminoantipyrine, 10 mM phenol, 10 AM FAD, 4 I.U. horse radish peroxidase, 0.2
mg bovine serum albumin, 50 AM palmitoyl-CoA in 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4).
Catalase (EC 1.11.1.6) activity was determined spectrophotometrically by the method of Aebi (1984),
measuring the enzymatic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Protein concentration was measured by
the method of Scopes (1996), modified by Lowry method (1951).

Statistical analysis

   All statistical analyses were carried out using ANOVA and Duncan’s multiple range test, p value of
b0.05 was selected as a limit of statistical significance. The statistical program used was SAS package
(Cary, NC, USA).


Results

Food intake and body and liver weights

  There were no significant differences in diet intake, final body weight, or weight increase rate among
10% fat-feeding experimental groups. Food intakes were not different within a group because rats were
individually housed and adapted to a 3-h feeding regimen. However, a significant hepatomegaly was
observed in fish oil group as indicated by the relative liver weight to body weight in a 4-week feeding
(Table 3).

Hepatic peroxisomal oxidation and catalase activity

  The activity of catalase, a marker enzyme of peroxisome, was significantly increased in 10% fat-fed
groups compared with 1% corn oil diet group (Table 4). Among the dietary fats, fish oil showed the
most stimulating effect in 4-day and 4-week feeding experiments. Perilla oil was more effective than
corn  oil  in 4-week experiment, although the difference was not  significant  in 4-day short-term
experiment. Peroxisomal h-oxidation was also markedly increased by fish oil feeding (Table 4). Perilla
oil slightly increased peroxisomal oxidation, but significant difference was not observed compared
with other fats.

Dawley rats were fed each of the experimental diets for 4 weeks and 4 days.

H.-K. Kim, H. Choi / Life Sciences 77 (2005) 1293–1306                       1301


differences among the rats fed beef tallow, corn oil, and 1% corn oil diet. However, n-3 PUFA sources
elevated hepatic acyl-CoA oxidase mRNA levels markedly. The increase was greater with fish oil than
perilla oil in a 4-week feeding experiment. The content of acyl-CoA oxidase mRNA was 4-fold in fish
oil group and 2.1-fold in perilla oil group compared with 1% corn oil diet group. Similarly, 2.9-fold in
fish oil group and 2.3-fold in perilla oil group were expressed in a 4-day feeding.

Postprandial plasma triacylglycerol level and hepatic triacylglycerol content

  The postprandial plasma and liver triacylglycerols were affected by dietary  fat (Table 5). The
concentrations of plasma triacylglycerol in fish oil- and perilla oil-fed groups were significantly lower
than the other groups in a 4-week feeding experiment. Similarly, the lowest value was found in fish oil-
fed group even in a 4-day feeding trial, followed by perilla oil and beef tallow-fed groups. Hepatic
triacylglycerol contents were low in perilla oil- and fish oil-fed groups compared with the other groups,
although there was no significant difference in total hepatic lipid contents. On the contrary, corn oil
feeding did not result in any significant decrease in plasma and liver triacylglycerol levels.

Fatty acid composition of hepatic membrane

  The fatty acids in the hepatic microsomal phospholipid reflected the fatty acid composition of dietary
fats (Table 6). The major fatty acids in rats fed the beef tallow diet were palmitic, stearic, and oleic acid.
Similarly, linoleic acid in corn oil-fed group, ALA in perilla oil-fed group, palmitic acid and DHA in fish
oil-fed group were detected in high proportion. In addition, fatty acids, not detected in dietary fat itself,
were shown in hepatic microsomal fractions in substantial amount. In corn oil-fed group, high content of
arachidonic acid (AA, C20:4, n-6) was detected, while low AA content was shown with the increase of
EPA and DHA in perilla oil-fed group. Perilla and fish oils increased the proportions of n-3 fatty acids
accompanying the decrease of n-6 fatty acids. Similar fatty acid composition was found in a 4-day feeding
experiment, although the extent of difference was not so great as in a 4-week feeding experiment.


Discussion

  Rats in experimental groups fed 10% fat consumed the same amount of calories, carbohydrate, and
other nutrients, so all the results can be considered as a sole effect of different dietary fats. Even though
there was no difference in body weight and rate of increase, a significant hepatomegaly was observed in
fish oil group as indicated by the relative liver weight to body weight. Fish oil was reported to induce
hepatic peroxisomal proliferation by increasing number, volume, and surface density of peroxisomes (De
Craeme et al., 1993). Peroxisomes are characterized by the presence of hydrogen peroxide producing
oxidase and high amounts of catalase catalyzing dismutation of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen
(Reddy and Mannaerts, 1994). Feeding the fish oil diet led to 133% increase of acyl-CoA oxidase
activity, while catalase showed 21% increase over corn oil diet. This disproportionate increase of acyl-
CoA oxidase activity compared to catalase may be an explanation for the hepatomegaly in the fish oil
fed group. The resultant hydrogen peroxide and reactive oxygen species might induce cell proliferation,
which  is supported by the reports showing the increase in ornithine decarboxylase and cytosolic
thymidine kinase activity (Chan et al., 1994; Ashby et al., 1995).

1302                          H.-K. Kim, H. Choi / Life Sciences 77 (2005) 1293–1306


  Numerous studies have shown that fish oil rich in very long chain n-3 fatty acids lower plasma
triacylglycerol levels in both fasting and postprandial state (Harris et al., 1988; Weintraub et al., 1988;
Harris, 1993; Agren et al., 1996). Our study confirmed that consumption of fish oil markedly reduced
postprandial triglyceridemia and perilla oil, another n-3 PUFA source, was also shown to be effective in
both 4-week and 4-day feeding experiments. Whether the hypotriglyceridemic effect of these n-3 PUFA
sources can be caused by similar physiological activity was our major concern. Plasma triacylglycerol
level is determined by the balance of fatty acid oxidation and lipogenesis, which is influenced dietary
macronutrient content (Parks and Parks, 2002). We used 1C diet with massive amount of carbohydrate as
a control to compare the additive effect of dietary fats. It has been reported that hypotriglyceridemic
effect of many hypolipidemic compounds is related to the peroxisome induction (Osumi and Hashimoto,
1979; Yamazaki et al., 1987).
   Fish oil feeding caused a conspicuous increase in the hepatic peroxisomal h-oxidation in postprandial
state, as reported in fasting state (Mohan et al., 1991; Vamecq et al., 1993; Kvannes et al., 1995).
Catalase, a peroxisomal enzyme not directly involved in h-oxidation, was measured as a control for total
peroxisomal  activity. Fish  oil-fed group showed the most stimulating  effect on catalase  activity
compared with other groups, which suggests that fish oil induce the peroxisomal activity. In addition, the
activity of acyl-CoA oxidase, the rate-limiting enzyme in peroxisomal h-oxidation, was also found to be
markedly induced by fish oil feeding. These results demonstrate that enhanced peroxisomal fatty acid
oxidation would be an important factor for postprandial hypotriglyceridemia in  rats fed fish  oil.
Considering that dietary EPA and DHA increased the activity of peroxisomal oxidation enzyme
(Aarslands et al., 1990; Kvannes et al., 1995; Berge et al., 1999), EPA and DHA seem to be major
contributors of hypotriglyceridemic effect of fish oil.
  On the other hand, in spite of the fact that perilla oil contains neither EPA nor DHA, perilla oil was
effective to reduce postprandial triglyceridemia. The analyses of fatty acid composition in the hepatic
microsomal phospholipid revealed that perilla oil resulted in high contents of EPA and DHA with low
content of AA. It is likely that this result was due to the effective desaturation and elongation of ALA to
long chain n-3 PUFA, especially EPA and to a lesser amount of DHA. This is consistent with other
studies showing considerable conversion of high doses of ALA to EPA, although they reported that
conversion to DHA was very restricted (Gester, 1998; Fu and Sinclair, 2000). Our study also showed that
plasma and hepatic triacylglycerol contents were negatively correlated with microsomal DHA content
(r =  0.613 for plasma TG; r =  0.629 for hepatic TG, p b0.05). Accordingly, a common mechanism by
which these oils reduce postprandial triacylglycerol could be considered.
  Peroxisomal h-oxidation in rats fed perilla oil was not significantly increased. This is contrary to other
reports that perilla oil compared to palm and safflower oil increased the peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation
activity (Ide et al., 1996; Kabir and Ide, 1996; Ide et al., 2000). This discrepancy might be ascribed to the
fat content of the diet. According to Kawashima and Kozuka (1993), hepatic peroxisomal h-oxidation in
rats fed perilla oil was not significantly different from that of safflower oil fed animals at medium fat
level (27% of energy), while a significant increase was found at high fat level (40% of energy). In
addition, total liver capacity for peroxisomal h-oxidation was increased with a higher fat content of the
diet (Ishii et al., 1980; Flatmark et al., 1983). These results indicate that fat content of the diet as well as
the composition of fat seems to play an important role to induce peroxisomal oxidation. Thus, moderate
fat level in our study (20% of energy) may cause the marginal increase of overall peroxisomal oxidation
in rats fed perilla oil. However, acyl-CoA oxidase activity of perilla oil group was increased compared
with that of corn oil group in a 4-day short-term feeding, although the significance disappeared as the

H.-K. Kim, H. Choi / Life Sciences 77 (2005) 1293–1306                       1303


feeding period was extended. The acyl-CoA oxidase activity was found to be positive correlated with
overall peroxisomal oxidation in our study (r =0.863 in a 4-day feeding experiment; r =0.705 in a 4-
week feeding experiment, p =0.0001). Statistical analyses in our study also revealed that the acyl-CoA
oxidase activity rather than overall peroxisomal h-oxidation was directly correlated with plasma and
hepatic triacylglycerol (r =  0.371 for plasma TG, r =  0.371 for hepatic TG, p b0.05 respectively in a
4-week feeding experiment; r =  0.512 for plasma TG in a 4-day feeding experiment, p =0.01). In
addition, a highly positive correlation was found between DHA content of hepatic membrane fraction
and acyl-CoA oxidase activity (r =0.924 in a 4-week feeding experiment; r =0.805 in a 4-day feeding
experiment, p b0.05). And, to a lesser degree, EPA was also correlated with acyl-CoA oxidase activity
(r =0.449 in a 4-day feeding experiment, p b0.01). These results suggest that perilla oil as well as fish oil
induce peroxisomal oxidation enzyme by enriching these very long chain n-3 PUFA.
  Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor a (PPARa) suggested to be a crucial PUFA responsive
factor in regulating peroxisomal oxidation enzyme gene expression (Keller et al., 1993; Forman et al.,
1997; Jump and Clarke, 1999). Cotransfection assays using cultured cells (Keller et al., 1993; Forman et
al., 1997) showed that PUFA activate PPAR more than saturated fatty acids do. However, various PUFA,
including linoleic, ALA, AA, EPA, and DHA, are equally effective in activating PPAR. In contrast to
this, animal experiments appeared differently as shown in the recent studies (Ide et al., 1996, 2000; Kabir
and Ide, 1996). In our study, fish and perilla oils rich in n-3 PUFA increased acyl-CoA mRNA content,
while corn oil rich in linoleic acid compared to saturated fats did not. This shows that n-3 PUFA can
induce gene expression of fatty acid oxidation enzyme, although the extent of increase was greater with
fish oil than with perilla oil. And no difference between corn oil and beef tallow may partly account for
the failure to reduce postprandial triacylglycerol following corn oil supplementation. There was a
positive correlation between acyl-CoA activity and relative amount of acyl-CoA oxidase mRNA
(r =0.714 in a 4-week feeding experiment; r =0.926 in a 4-day feeding experiment, p b0.01) in our
study. This result suggests that the increase of enzyme activity should be mostly mediated by an increase
of enzyme synthesis rate.
  Another interesting result was the different response of fish and perilla oils with the duration of
feeding. The effect of fish oil on the activity and gene expression of acyl-CoA oxidase was intensified
as the feeding period was extended. On the other hand, stimulating effect of perilla oil was apparent in
a 4-day feeding, but gradually decreased with the longer periods of fat feeding. Therefore, some
adaptive mechanisms seem  to  affect  differently  as  the  feeding  period was  extended.  Partially
hydrogenated marine oils rich in EPA and DHA were reported to increase the activity by reducing the
rate of acyl-CoA oxidase degradation (Horie and Suga, 1989). It is worthwhile to consider the effect
of fatty acids on acyl-CoA oxidase degradation rate as a possible factor to cause different response of
these two oils. Further studies are required to clarify this possibility because the effect of perilla oil
has not been reported yet. In addition, considering that perilla oil effectively reduced postprandial
triacylglycerol in spite of comparable peroxisomal activity compared with corn oil in the long-term
experiment,  the  stimulation  of  peroxisomal  h-oxidation may  not be  sufficient  to  explain  the
postprandial hypotriglyceridemia in rats fed ALA. It cannot be ruled out that the decreased synthesis
of fatty acids in VLDL-TG production and secretion may be a more significant contributor to the
hypolipidemic effect of perilla oil.
   In conclusion, dietary perilla oil and fish oil exert a similar activity in modulating hepatic activity and
gene expression of acyl-CoA oxidase by accumulation of EPA and DHA in hepatic membrane fraction.
This can be partly accounted for the reduction of postprandial triacylglycerol concentration.
